analysis.one_liner: Ties COVID-19 hospital relief money to keeping nurses employed and paid.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee without a vote after being referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee in May 2020.
analysis.plain_summary: During the COVID-19 pandemic, the federal government sent hospitals and other health providers billions in relief through the CARES Act. This bill would have conditioned that money: any provider taking it had to keep at least 75% of its nurses employed, keep average nurse pay and hours at 75% of pre-pandemic levels, and not force nurses onto leave for two months after getting the funds. Providers that broke the agreement would have to repay the money in full.
analysis.who_benefits: Nurses — registered nurses, licensed practical and vocational nurses, and advanced practice nurses — working at providers that took federal COVID-19 relief money. It protected their jobs, pay, and hours during a period when providers were cutting staff even as they received emergency funds, and it indirectly protected patients by keeping staffing levels up.

how_it_helps.text: Providers receiving COVID-19 relief funds had to keep at least 75% of the nurses they employed as of January 31, 2020.

They also had to maintain average nurse pay and average paid hours at no less than 75% of pre-pandemic levels, and could not require nurses to take paid or unpaid leave, for two months after receiving funds.
Providers that violated the agreement would have had to repay 100% of the relief disbursement.
Providers that had already cut nurse staffing, pay, or hours before receiving funds got a 30-day window to restore them before the requirements took effect.

analysis.who_pays: Hospitals and other health care providers that received COVID-19 relief money. They would face restrictions on how they managed nurse staffing and pay for two months, and would repay relief funds in full if they cut nurses below the required thresholds.

drawbacks.text: The requirements were narrow: they covered only a two-month window after each disbursement and allowed providers to cut nurse pay, hours, and staffing by up to 25% while still keeping the relief money.

Hospitals argued (in the broader debate over relief conditions) that pandemic revenue losses forced staffing and pay decisions, and repayment penalties could strain providers already facing financial distress; the bill offered no additional funding to cover the cost of maintaining payrolls.
The bill applied only to nurses, leaving other frontline health workers without similar protections.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protections were real but modest: a two-month staffing and pay floor tied to money providers were already receiving, with a 25% cut allowance and full repayment as the only penalty. For nurses facing layoffs and pay cuts during a pandemic, it would have provided meaningful short-term protection at little cost to taxpayers, since the money was already appropriated. The design was narrow and temporary rather than a lasting staffing standard.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in May 2020 and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, which never acted on it, and the bill died when that Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Rep. Rodney Davis (R-IL) introduced the Nurse Workforce Protection Act of 2020 on May 12, 2020, with Rep. Tulsi Gabbard as the bill's cosponsor.
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce, and no further action was taken.
The 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021, and the bill expired without a floor vote or committee markup.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Hospitals and health providers that received COVID-19 relief funds came out ahead: they were never bound by the staffing, pay, and leave conditions or the repayment requirement, and could manage nurse employment as they chose.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Relief-funded hospitals, whose staffing stayed unregulated

for.name: Rep. Rodney Davis
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill tying COVID-19 relief funds to nurse staffing and pay protections.

for.name: Rep. Tulsi Gabbard
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it bipartisan sponsorship.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never scheduled a markup or advanced it, leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had one Republican sponsor and one Democratic cosponsor, but with only two members behind it, neither party mobilized to move it.

industries.note: The bill would have conditioned COVID-19 relief money on keeping nurses employed and paid, with full repayment for violations, restricting the industry's freedom to cut staffing and pay while using public funds. Providers receiving relief funds benefits from the bill's failure to advance.

Nurses stood to gain job, pay, and hour protections tied to relief funds, but the two-month window and 25% cut allowance limited the benefit. Their interests ran alongside those of patients who depend on staffing levels.
